title: Instrument identification and handling

related.id: MB-143 Excision of a skin lesion

brief.scenario: A tray of common surgical instruments, blades and suture packets is laid out for a minor operations list. The examiner will describe the items on it to you.
brief.task: The examiner will read out descriptions of the instruments. Name each one and say what it is for, describe how you would hold it, describe how you would load and remove a scalpel blade safely, and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Name it, say what it's for, say how you hold it, and treat every sharp as dangerous.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Saying you would load or remove a blade with your fingers.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Name the needle holder before you describe touching a blade.

flow: Name cutting instruments from the descriptions
Describe loading and removing a blade

grid.label: Cutting instruments
grid.fail: Mixes up handles and blades from the descriptions.
grid.pass: No. 3 handle with blades 10, 11 and 15; No. 4 handle with blades 20–25; Mayo and Metzenbaum scissors.
grid.high: Matches blade to handle before opening: No. 3 takes the small blades (e.g. 10, 11, 15); No. 4 takes the large blades (18–27).

grid.label: Holding and retracting instruments
grid.pass: Toothed and non-toothed forceps, needle holder, artery forceps, Langenbeck retractor.
grid.high: Explains use: toothed forceps for skin, non-toothed for bowel and vessels, Babcock for bowel, self-retainers for deeper exposure.

grid.label: Loading and removing a blade (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Would load or remove the blade with fingers.
grid.pass: Describes using a needle holder, blade pointing away and down, matching the blade to the handle's groove.
grid.high: Would use a blade remover where available and dispose into a sharps bin at the point of use.

grid.label: Grips
grid.fail: Describes fingers deep in the needle holder's rings, with no control.
grid.pass: Describes holding scalpel like a pen or table knife as appropriate, forceps like a pen, needle holder with thumb and ring finger.
grid.high: Uses the index finger to steady the needle holder, and describes releasing the ratchet smoothly.

grid.label: Passing sharps (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Would pass a scalpel hand to hand.
grid.pass: Would pass sharps in a tray (neutral zone), saying 'sharp' as they do.
grid.high: Knows instrument, swab and needle counts are part of the sign-out in the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.

grid.label: Sutures
grid.pass: Absorbable: polyglactin, poliglecaprone, polydioxanone. Non-absorbable: polypropylene, nylon.
grid.high: Matches choice to tissue, e.g. non-absorbable monofilament for interrupted skin sutures, slowly absorbed polydioxanone for mass closure.

grid.label: Sharps injury response
grid.fail: Doesn't know what to do after a needlestick.
grid.pass: Encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water, don't suck the wound, report it, contact occupational health.
grid.high: Knows the source patient's risk is assessed promptly because post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Items 1 and 2, and the blades: what are they?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you load the blade?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd push it onto the handle with my fingers.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you pass it to me?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd hand it to you, blade first.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Items 1 and 2, and the blades: what are they?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Item 1 is a No. 3 scalpel handle; it takes blades 10, 11 and 15. The larger item 2 is a No. 4 handle, which takes blades 20 to 25. The two pairs of scissors are Mayo and, the finer ones, Metzenbaum.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Toothed forceps, non-toothed forceps, a needle holder, artery forceps and a Langenbeck retractor.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you load a blade?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd grip the blade with the needle holder, pointing away and down, and slide it onto the groove. I'd remove it the same way.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Scalpel like a pen, forceps like a pen, needle holder with thumb and ring finger.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you pass me the scalpel?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd place it in a kidney dish and say 'sharp'.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Which of these sutures are absorbable?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Polyglactin, poliglecaprone and polydioxanone are absorbable; polypropylene and nylon are not.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: You get a needlestick. What do you do?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Encourage bleeding, wash under running water, don't suck it, report it and contact occupational health.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Items 1 and 2, and the blades: what are they?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Item 1 is a No. 3 handle, for blades 10, 11 and 15: the 15 for small skin lesions, the 11 for stab incisions, the 10 for longer skin incisions. Item 2, the No. 4, takes 20 to 25, like the large broad blade. Mayo scissors for heavier tissue and sutures, Metzenbaum for fine dissection.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Toothed forceps for skin, non-toothed for bowel and vessels, a needle holder, artery forceps, a Babcock for holding bowel, and a Langenbeck retractor; I'd use a self-retainer for deeper exposure.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you load a blade?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: With a needle holder, blade pointing away and down, onto the groove. To remove it I'd use a blade remover if there is one, and dispose of it straight into the sharps bin.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Pen grip for scalpel and forceps; thumb and ring finger in the needle holder, index finger steadying it; and I release the ratchet smoothly.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you pass me the scalpel?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In a kidney dish, saying 'sharp'. And at the end, the instrument, swab and needle counts are part of the sign-out.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Non-absorbable monofilament like nylon or polypropylene for interrupted skin sutures; slowly absorbed polydioxanone for mass closure of the abdomen.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Encourage bleeding, wash, report and go to occupational health straight away, because the source patient's risk needs assessing quickly in case post-exposure prophylaxis is needed.

failures.move: Describing fingers deep in the needle holder's rings.
failures.consequence: Poor control and clumsy release of the ratchet.

failures.move: Passing a scalpel hand to hand.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: exposes you and the assistant to a sharps injury; use a neutral zone or tray.

recovery.line: I'm not sure of its name. From its rounded, fenestrated head and ratchet, I think it's used to hold bowel, so a Babcock.

recovery.when: You start to say you'd handle a blade with your fingers
recovery.line: Stop: I'll use the needle holder for that.

knowledge.fact: No. 3 handle takes blades 10, 11, 12 and 15; No. 4 handle takes blades 18 to 27, including 20 to 25.
Employers must have safe systems for using and disposing of sharps and for responding to sharps injuries.
Counts of instruments, swabs and needles are confirmed at sign-out.

recall.think: Every sharp is dangerous; name it, use it, hold it.
do: Load and remove blades with a needle holder
recall.finish: Right instrument, right grip, sharps never hand to hand.

sources.name: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: At every station: introduce yourself, explain the task, confirm identity, obtain consent, clean hands before and after patient contact; 6-minute signal in examination stations

partner.opening: I'm going to read out descriptions of the instruments on the tray. Name each one and tell me what it's for.

reveals.finding: Read out: item 1 is a flat steel handle with a small, narrow blade fitting at its tip. Item 2 is a similar but heavier handle with a larger, broader fitting. There are four loose blades: one with a small curved cutting edge; one triangular, with a straight cutting edge and a sharp point; one with a longer curved cutting edge; and one large, broad blade with a long curved edge. There are two pairs of scissors: one sturdy pair with heavy, slightly curved blades; and one pair with long, slender handles and short, fine, blunt-tipped blades.

Read out: item 3 is a pair of spring forceps with interlocking teeth at the tips. Item 4 is a similar pair with fine serrations and no teeth. Item 5 is a ringed, ratcheted instrument with short, stout jaws that carry a cross-hatched gripping surface. Item 6 is a ringed, ratcheted instrument with slender jaws, serrated across their full length. Item 7 is a ringed, ratcheted instrument whose jaws end in a rounded, triangular, fenestrated head that does not crush. Item 8 is a hand-held retractor: a handle ending in a flat blade bent at a right angle.

reveals.trigger: Ask them to load the blade
reveals.finding: Listen for whether they use a needle holder.

reveals.trigger: Ask how they would pass you the scalpel
reveals.finding: Offer to take it from their hand; listen for whether they use the tray instead.

push.question: Describe how you hold a needle holder.
push.expect: Thumb and ring finger, index finger steadying.

push.question: What do you do after a needlestick?
push.expect: Bleed, wash, report, occupational health promptly.

curveballs.prompt: Just put the scalpel in my hand.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Uses the tray and says 'sharp' rather than passing hand to hand.

curveballs.prompt: There's no blade remover on the tray.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Remove the blade with a needle holder, pointing away, straight into the sharps bin.
